facts.F1:
ADO User Story 6712 "Faster page loads on slow connections: compression, shared cache, smaller update check", as written on the board:

On a slow connection, Lighthouse pages take 8–20 s to show their data on a first visit, and 5–9 s when you click to a Team or Portfolio page. A measuring spike (2026-11-27, docs/feature/api-shape-evaluation/spike/findings.md) found that most of that time is spent sending uncompressed JavaScript, not on the number of API calls.

Fixes found by the spike
- Compression. The frontend is served with UseStaticFiles, which ignores the .gz files the build already makes, and API answers are not compressed. JavaScript: 3.4 MB raw vs 1.0 MB compressed. Expected gain on slow 4G: about 4–10 s per page.
- One shared cache for data every page uses. useRbac fetches the user's permissions once per component that uses it (72 repeated calls over 16 pages). Teams, portfolios, licence and Team settings repeat for similar reasons.
- A smaller update check. GET /version/new sends 368 KB of release notes on every first visit, only to show whether an update exists.
- Parallel version checks. The version footer runs 5 independent checks one after another.

No visible UI change; pages show the same data, sooner. Measure before and after with the spike's probe (measure-calls.mjs, measure-bytes.mjs).

Separate from the GraphQL / API-shape evaluation, which continues on its own and ends in an ADR.

facts.F351: Open question 1 resolved (compression of the built frontend): compress at serve time with ASP.NET Core ResponseCompression (shared framework, no new package), Brotli and Gzip providers both at CompressionLevel.Optimal, never SmallestSize (Brotli quality 11 is about 140 times slower: 3510 ms against 25 ms on the 2.43 MB largest JavaScript file, x86_64). No size threshold: a threshold can only act where Content-Length is known, which is the static files, where compression pays most. app.UseResponseCompression placed after UseForwardedHeaders and before UseDefaultFiles/UseStaticFiles so static files, the SPA fallback page and API answers pass through one mechanism. UseStaticFiles(staticFileOptions) and the UseSpa DefaultPageStaticFileOptions stay unchanged, so index.html and sw.js keep no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate on both paths. Measured on the current bundle (3361 KB of JavaScript): Optimal gives 3.22x gzip and 3.23x Brotli; Fastest gives only 2.32x gzip, which misses the about-a-third outcome. Server CPU is about 35 ms per cold load of the bundle in one encoding (measured in DEVOPS, x86_64). Rejected: MapStaticAssets (needs the static web assets manifest built after pnpm build fills wwwroot, replaces the StaticFileOptions path that the no-cache rule lives on, and is empty in dev); a Vite precompression plugin plus a custom precompressed-file provider (new dependency and hand-written content negotiation to save about 35 ms CPU per cold load).
facts.F352: Open question 2 resolved (BREACH): an answer is compressed only when ResponseCompression:Enabled is true, the request method is GET or HEAD, the response MIME type is in ResponseCompressionDefaults.MimeTypes, the client sent Accept-Encoding with br or gzip, and the path is not an excluded route. Excluded routes, matched on path segments, case-insensitive, by prefix: the SignalR hub api/updateNotificationHub (and everything under it, such as negotiate); the logs controller api/{v1|latest}/logs (tail, download, problems, level), because its answers hold log text an attacker can reach (logged paths, failed sign-ins, tracker queries) next to exception text from third-party libraries that this design cannot show is free of secrets, and an administrator can raise the log level at run time; and the embed handshake api/{v1|latest}/embed/handshake, the one GET whose body carries a secret (the single-use embed session token). The handshake body reflects no attacker text and its nonce is spent on first read, so it is not exploitable today; it is excluded so the rule stays simple: no compressed answer carries a secret, and the answer is a few hundred bytes. Every other GET carries no secret: connection options blank secret values (WorkTrackingSystemConnectionOptionDto sets Value empty when IsSecret), GET api-keys never returns the plaintext (ApiKeyController.GetApiKeys), the OAuth callback answers a redirect with a connection id, session and embed cookies travel in headers, which ResponseCompression never compresses; the plain-text API key of ApiKeyCreationResult answers a POST. The embed cookie is SameSite=None, so cross-site GETs carry it; no GET in embed scope other than the excluded handshake returns a token. EnableForHttps is true because the rule, not the scheme, is the mitigation, so TLS at a proxy does not change the answer. Owner in code: BreachSafeResponseCompressionProvider in Platform/Host, a subclass of ResponseCompressionProvider overriding ShouldCompressResponse; the hub route is one named constant on UpdateNotificationHub read by both MapHub and the policy; the logs and handshake prefixes are named constants in the provider. No PathBase is used, so the segments are matched on Request.Path. Platform facts (DEVOPS): the Docker image serves HTTPS 443 with nothing in front; the Helm chart's plain Ingress (ingress-nginx, Traefik) does not compress by default and passes an already encoded answer through; a proxy that strips Accept-Encoding gets identity answers; the Standalone webview loads its UI from the app bundle and only its loopback API answers are compressed, about 1 ms each; one behaviour everywhere.
facts.F353: S1 switch: ResponseCompressionConfiguration in Configuration/ResponseCompressionConfiguration.cs (SectionName ResponseCompression, Enabled default true), read once at start-up in Program.cs the way RateLimitingConfiguration is (GetSection(SectionName).Get, else a new instance), registered as a singleton and given to BreachSafeResponseCompressionProvider, which answers no for every request when Enabled is false, so the switch is one row of the policy table and the pipeline shape is the same either way. Environment variable ResponseCompression__Enabled=false or --ResponseCompression:Enabled=false; a restart is needed; no Helm chart value. docs/Installation/configuration.md gets one section in the format of the Telemetry block: Lighthouse compresses its own answers, a reverse proxy needs no compression of its own, and how to turn it off.
facts.F354: S1 accepted behaviours: an identity answer to a request without Accept-Encoding carries no Vary header (never wrong; at worst a shared cache serves identity to a client that could take br); StaticFiles gives one strong ETag for every encoding (harmless with Vary, no CDN in the repository); application/problem+json and image/svg+xml stay uncompressed because they are not on the default MIME list. Usage data: N/A, because nothing here is a user action; the outcome (bytes and calls per page) is measured by the spike's probes, so no UsageDataEventName entry. Observability: the Content-Encoding and Vary response headers show it is on; no metric or alert, because no service-level promise changes.
facts.F355: S1 test layers: unit rows in the default fast suite (no host) pin the rule as a table over DefaultHttpContext in BreachSafeResponseCompressionProviderTest; one named wire contract (ResponseCompressionWireContractTest on WireContractTest) pins pipeline order and headers through a real host; the Docker smoke step in .github/workflows/ci_docker.yml, after Check the container runs on .NET 11, covers real TLS and the real bundle: curl -k a built asset with Accept-Encoding br and fail unless content-encoding is br, and curl /api/latest/systeminfo without Accept-Encoding and fail if content-encoding is present. facts.F77: Formal verification: claim-to-checker. Shared-read freshness (S2, S3: one request per page, no earlier-page answer for a new component, cancelled earlier-page requests, own change asked at once) has several actors (components, navigation, network, user) on one cache, so it is modelled in Quint (shared_page_reads.qnt), checked with quint run and quint verify (Apalache, bounded). No model for compression and the BREACH rule: a pure decision over one request with no shared state or multi-step protocol; its finite table is checked by unit rows and the wire contract. No model for the Features tab read: removal of an unread fetch, no state window. No model for the parallel version checks: a single Promise.all with one shared error flag, no shared mutable state between actors; finite example rows cover any-failure. Liveness: no liveness claim, because eventual arrival of a page’s answer depends on the HTTP answer arriving, which this design does not control; safety is the claim. No TLA+ or Agda needed.
facts.F78: Tests: Lighthouse test-writing skill wins over nWave test rules (nine-run timing, PBT density). Frontend rules on hooks in .test.ts/.test.tsx with renderWithQueryClient; backend S1 is a wire contract on WireContractTest because only a running host shows Content-Encoding and headers produced by middleware order; the policy rule itself is pinned by unit rows on BreachSafeResponseCompressionProvider over DefaultHttpContext. No nWave tags in test code.
facts.F79: Page-move freshness (S2, S3): one owner, usePageFreshQuery in src/hooks/usePageFreshQuery.ts, wraps useQuery with staleTime Infinity, retry false and refetchOnMount false; its queryFn stores the answer together with the page it was asked on (carrier PageFreshAnswer of T: answer and askedOnPage). PageMoveRefresh in src/components/App/PageMoveRefresh/PageMoveRefresh.tsx, mounted inside the Router in App.tsx, holds the page counter (per-process state, a React context), advances it when location.pathname changes and invalidates the shared page reads once (invalidateQueries cancels a request still in flight from the previous page). A component records the page it mounted on; it is loading until an answer asked on or after that page arrives, failed when the shared query failed, ready otherwise. Components mounted later on the same page reuse the cached answer and ask nothing. Model shared_page_reads.qnt checks this protocol.
